title: Renal physiology — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Physiology Renal System lecture + syllabus

questions.stem: The kidneys are described as retroperitoneal, meaning they lie

options.label: A
options.text: behind the peritoneum on the posterior abdominal wall

options.label: B
options.text: within the peritoneal cavity among the intestines

options.label: C
options.text: inside the true pelvis below the bladder

options.label: D
options.text: within the thoracic cavity above the diaphragm

options.label: E
options.text: suspended freely in the greater omentum

questions.why: Retroperitoneal organs lie outside the peritoneal cavity, posterior to the parietal peritoneum. The kidneys lie against the posterior abdominal wall on either side of the vertebral column, surrounded by fat and renal fascia.

notes.B: Intraperitoneal organs such as the jejunum are largely covered by visceral peritoneum, unlike kidneys lying behind the parietal peritoneum.
notes.C: The bladder occupies the pelvis when empty, whereas the kidneys lie higher on the posterior abdominal wall.
notes.D: The thoracic cavity contains the lungs and mediastinal structures; the kidneys are abdominal organs below the diaphragm.
notes.E: The greater omentum hangs from the stomach and covers abdominal viscera; the kidneys are not suspended within it.

questions.stem: The right kidney normally lies slightly lower than the left because

options.label: A
options.text: the aorta displaces the left kidney up

options.label: B
options.text: the liver pushes the right kidney down

options.label: C
options.text: the spleen pushes the left kidney down

options.label: D
options.text: the right renal artery is longer

options.label: E
options.text: the right kidney is larger and heavier

questions.why: The large right lobe of the liver occupies space superior to the right kidney, accounting for its slightly lower position. Both kidneys lie retroperitoneally, with their levels varying somewhat during respiration.

notes.A: The abdominal aorta lies anterior to the vertebral column and does not normally push the left kidney upwards.
notes.C: The spleen relates to the upper left kidney, but the usual asymmetry is explained by the larger right hepatic lobe.
notes.D: The right renal artery is longer because the aorta lies left of the midline, not because it determines kidney height.
notes.E: Kidney size varies among individuals; the normal difference in position is primarily related to neighbouring organs rather than weight.

questions.stem: Urine formed in the kidney drains in the sequence

options.label: A
options.text: collecting duct, ureter, renal pelvis, calyx

options.label: B
options.text: renal pelvis, ureter, major calyx, bladder

options.label: C
options.text: minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter

options.label: D
options.text: renal pelvis, minor calyx, major calyx, ureter

options.label: E
options.text: major calyx, minor calyx, renal pelvis, ureter

questions.why: Papillary ducts discharge urine at the renal papilla into a minor calyx. Minor calyces unite into major calyces, which drain into the renal pelvis and then the ureter for transport to the bladder.

notes.A: Collecting ducts precede the calyces and renal pelvis; the ureter receives urine only after it passes through the pelvis.
notes.B: The renal pelvis drains into the ureter, but major calyces are upstream of the pelvis, not between the ureter and bladder.
notes.D: Minor and major calyces collect urine before it reaches the renal pelvis, rather than receiving urine after pelvic drainage.
notes.E: Minor calyces receive urine directly from renal papillae and unite into major calyces, so their proposed order is reversed.

questions.stem: Each human kidney contains approximately how many nephrons?
questions.why: Each human kidney contains roughly one million nephrons, with 1.25 million a conventional teaching estimate. Nephron number varies widely among individuals; each nephron includes a renal corpuscle and its associated tubule.

notes.A: A count of 125 million is approximately two orders of magnitude above the usual nephron number in one human kidney.
notes.B: Twelve thousand is far below the usual approximately million-nephron complement of an adult kidney.
notes.C: Two hundred and fifty nephrons would provide only a tiny fraction of the normal complement of functioning renal filtration units.
notes.E: Twenty-five thousand is substantially below the typical human nephron count, even allowing for considerable individual variation.

questions.stem: Juxtamedullary nephrons, about 15% of the total, differ from cortical nephrons in that they have

options.label: A
options.text: short loops of Henle confined to the cortex

options.label: B
options.text: no loop of Henle at all

options.label: C
options.text: glomeruli located in the outer cortex

options.label: E
options.text: long loops of Henle that dip deep into the medulla

questions.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons have renal corpuscles near the corticomedullary junction and long loops extending deep into the medulla. Their loops and associated vasa recta help establish and preserve the medullary osmotic gradient needed to concentrate urine.

notes.A: Short loops extending only into the outer medulla are typical of many cortical nephrons, rather than the long-looped juxtamedullary population.
notes.B: Juxtamedullary nephrons possess loops of Henle; their extensive medullary penetration is particularly important for urinary concentration.
notes.C: Glomeruli in the superficial cortex are characteristic of cortical nephrons, whereas juxtamedullary glomeruli lie close to the medulla.
notes.D: Both cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons possess juxtaglomerular apparatuses for regulation of renin secretion and glomerular filtration.

questions.stem: The vasa recta, the hairpin capillaries running alongside the loop of Henle, arise from the efferent arterioles of
questions.why: Efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary glomeruli give rise to descending vasa recta, which form medullary capillary networks and ascending return vessels. Their countercurrent arrangement supplies the medulla while limiting washout of its osmotic gradient.

notes.B: Cortical efferent arterioles predominantly form peritubular capillary networks around cortical tubules rather than the long medullary vasa recta.
notes.C: Afferent arterioles deliver blood into glomeruli; medullary vasa recta arise downstream of the glomerular capillary bed.
notes.D: Arcuate veins collect venous blood near the corticomedullary junction and are not the arterial source of descending vasa recta.
notes.E: Peritubular venules collect blood from capillary networks; vasa recta receive their arterial inflow from juxtamedullary efferent arterioles.

questions.stem: Within the juxtaglomerular apparatus, the cells that actually produce and secrete renin are the

options.label: A
options.text: principal cells of the collecting duct

options.label: B
options.text: granular cells of the afferent arteriole

options.label: C
options.text: macula densa cells of the distal tubule

questions.why: Juxtaglomerular granular cells are modified vascular smooth-muscle cells located mainly in the afferent arteriolar wall near the glomerulus. They synthesise, store and release renin in response to signals such as reduced perfusion pressure.

notes.A: Collecting-duct principal cells regulate sodium, potassium and water transport under hormonal control rather than synthesising circulating renin.
notes.C: Macula densa cells detect tubular sodium chloride and signal nearby granular cells, but are not the principal renin-producing cells.
notes.D: Extraglomerular mesangial cells participate in signalling and structural organisation of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, rather than serving as its main renin source.
notes.E: Podocytes form the visceral epithelium of the renal corpuscle and contribute to filtration selectivity rather than producing renin.

questions.stem: The macula densa, part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, functions to

options.label: A
options.text: reabsorb glucose in the proximal tubule

options.label: C
options.text: sense the NaCl in the distal tubular fluid

options.label: D
options.text: secrete renin into the afferent arteriole

questions.why: Macula densa cells at the end of the thick ascending limb detect luminal sodium chloride delivery through NKCC2. Their signals influence afferent arteriolar tone and granular-cell renin release, linking tubular delivery to glomerular filtration.

notes.A: Proximal tubular epithelial cells reabsorb filtered glucose using sodium–glucose cotransporters; macula densa cells instead monitor distal sodium chloride delivery.
notes.B: Renal erythropoietin is produced mainly by specialised interstitial fibroblast-like cells responding to hypoxia, rather than macula densa cells.
notes.D: Granular cells in the juxtaglomerular arteriolar wall secrete renin; the macula densa regulates them through local signals.
notes.E: The glomerular endothelial, basement membrane and podocyte barrier filters plasma; macula densa cells monitor tubular fluid after filtration.

questions.stem: Besides producing renin and erythropoietin, the kidney contributes to mineral homeostasis by

options.label: D
options.text: converting vitamin D to its active form

questions.why: Renal proximal tubular cells express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). This hormone promotes intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and contributes to regulation of mineral balance.

notes.A: Calcitonin is produced by thyroid parafollicular cells, rather than being the major renal hormone involved in calcium metabolism.
notes.B: Medullary calcium deposition is not a normal endocrine mechanism; the kidney regulates mineral balance through transport and calcitriol synthesis.
notes.C: Thyroid follicular cells synthesise thyroid hormones, which regulate metabolism, rather than the kidney producing them to control calcium.
notes.E: Parathyroid glands produce parathyroid hormone, which stimulates renal calcitriol synthesis; the kidney itself is not its principal source.

questions.stem: The yellow colour of normal urine is due mainly to the pigment
questions.why: The characteristic yellow colour of normal urine is largely attributable to urochrome pigments, including urobilin derived from bilirubin metabolism. Urinary concentration influences the intensity of the colour, producing darker urine when water conservation increases.

notes.A: Conjugated bilirubin can darken urine in hepatobiliary disease, but it is not the principal pigment giving normal urine its yellow colour.
notes.B: Biliverdin is a green intermediate of haem degradation, rather than the usual yellow urinary pigment derived downstream of bilirubin metabolism.
notes.C: Melanin contributes to pigmentation of skin and other tissues, rather than producing the usual yellow colour of normal urine.
notes.D: Carotenoids contribute to yellow-orange pigmentation in certain tissues, but normal urinary yellow colour is principally attributed to urochrome pigments.

questions.stem: Urine that has been left to stand develops an ammonia smell because
questions.why: When urine stands, urease-producing microorganisms can hydrolyse urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. Ammonia gives the specimen a pungent odour and can increase its pH, particularly when storage permits bacterial growth.

notes.B: Volatile ketones can contribute a fruity odour in ketosis, rather than producing the characteristic ammoniacal smell of aged urine.
notes.C: Oxidation of urinary pigments may change colour, but ammonia generation requires breakdown of nitrogen-containing compounds such as urea.
notes.D: Urea hydrolysis generates ammonia and tends to increase urine pH, rather than causing a rapid fall below pH 4.
notes.E: Carbon dioxide escape may influence acid–base balance of the sample, but does not itself produce the characteristic ammonia odour.

questions.stem: A sweet or fruity odour of the urine suggests the presence of

options.label: C
options.text: excess urea from a high-protein diet

questions.why: Ketosis increases ketone-body production, and volatile acetone can contribute a sweet or fruity smell to urine. This may occur in uncontrolled diabetes or fasting, but odour alone cannot establish the cause or diagnose ketoacidosis.

notes.A: Urinary infections may produce unpleasant or ammoniacal odours, whereas a fruity smell is more suggestive of volatile ketone compounds.
notes.C: Increased urea excretion can contribute to ammonia formation after bacterial breakdown, rather than directly generating a characteristic fruity odour.
notes.D: Blood in urine may change its colour and indicate urinary tract pathology, but haematuria does not specifically cause a ketone-like fruity smell.
notes.E: Bile pigments may produce dark urine in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, rather than the characteristic sweet smell associated with ketone production.

questions.stem: The solute present in the highest concentration in normal urine is
questions.why: Urea is usually the most abundant individual nitrogenous urinary solute and is commonly the largest individual solute by mass in typical urine. Its concentration depends on dietary protein, renal handling and urine water content.

notes.A: Potassium excretion varies with intake and distal nephron regulation, but its typical mass concentration is below that of urea.
notes.B: Chloride is a major urinary electrolyte and contributes substantially to osmolality, but typical urinary urea concentration by mass is greater.
notes.D: Creatinine is excreted from muscle creatine metabolism and is useful for clearance estimates, but its urinary mass concentration is usually lower than urea.
notes.E: Sodium excretion varies substantially with dietary salt and hormonal regulation, whereas urea is generally the largest individual urinary solute by mass.

questions.stem: The specific gravity of normal urine ranges approximately from
questions.why: Urine specific gravity compares urine density with that of water and reflects the concentration and molecular mass of dissolved substances. A broad physiological range is approximately 1.001–1.035, depending on hydration and measurement conditions.

notes.A: A specific gravity of 1.100–1.200 is well above ordinary physiological urine concentration and suggests an unusual measurement or sample composition.
notes.B: Values of 0.800–0.950 indicate a density substantially below water, which is not expected for ordinary aqueous urine containing dissolved solutes.
notes.C: Values of 1.300–1.400 greatly exceed the usual concentrating capacity of the kidney and are not a normal urinary range.
notes.E: A value near 1.000 approaches water density, while values substantially below it do not represent the usual range of normal urine.

questions.stem: The smooth muscle of the bladder wall responsible for expelling urine is the
questions.why: The detrusor is the smooth-muscle coat of the urinary bladder. Parasympathetic activation contracts this muscle during micturition, raising intravesical pressure while coordinated reduction of outlet resistance permits urine to flow through the urethra.

notes.A: The psoas is a posterior abdominal wall skeletal muscle involved in hip flexion, rather than generating bladder emptying pressure.
notes.B: The cremaster elevates the testis through skeletal-muscle contraction and is not a component of the urinary bladder wall.
notes.C: Levator ani supports the pelvic organs and contributes to continence, but does not constitute the bladder's main contractile wall.
notes.D: The trigone is a smooth region of bladder mucosa between ureteric and urethral openings, rather than the principal expelling muscle.

questions.stem: The external urethral sphincter differs from the internal one in that it is

options.label: A
options.text: voluntary skeletal muscle via the pudendal nerve

options.label: C
options.text: smooth muscle controlled by the pelvic nerve

options.label: D
options.text: cardiac muscle supplied by the vagus

options.label: E
options.text: formed from the detrusor muscle itself

questions.why: The external urethral sphincter consists of striated skeletal muscle supplied by somatic motor pathways, predominantly through the pudendal nerve from sacral segments. Its voluntary activity supports continence and relaxes during coordinated voiding.

notes.B: Sympathetically regulated smooth muscle contributes to bladder-neck closure, whereas the external sphincter is a somatically controlled striated muscle.
notes.C: Pelvic parasympathetic nerves regulate detrusor activity and urethral relaxation, but the external sphincter is controlled principally through somatic motor pathways.
notes.D: Cardiac muscle is confined to the heart; the urethral sphincter is striated skeletal muscle, not vagally supplied cardiac tissue.
notes.E: The detrusor is bladder wall smooth muscle, anatomically and functionally distinct from the external striated urethral sphincter.

questions.stem: Parasympathetic fibres reaching the bladder through the pelvic nerves (S2-S4) act to

options.label: A
options.text: contract only the external urethral sphincter

options.label: B
options.text: contract the detrusor and relax the internal sphincter

options.label: C
options.text: relax the detrusor and contract the internal sphincter

options.label: D
options.text: contract both the detrusor and the internal sphincter

options.label: E
options.text: relax both the detrusor and the internal sphincter

questions.why: Sacral parasympathetic fibres promote voiding by releasing acetylcholine onto detrusor muscarinic receptors and facilitating smooth-muscle urethral relaxation through inhibitory pathways. Coordinated withdrawal of sympathetic and somatic outlet activity further reduces resistance to urine flow.

notes.A: External sphincter contraction is mediated primarily by somatic pudendal motor pathways and promotes continence rather than parasympathetic bladder emptying.
notes.C: Detrusor relaxation and bladder-neck contraction favour urine storage and are characteristic of sympathetic rather than parasympathetic voiding responses.
notes.D: Contraction of the bladder outlet would oppose urine expulsion; normal voiding coordinates detrusor contraction with reduced urethral resistance.
notes.E: Relaxation of the detrusor would fail to generate effective voiding pressure even if the bladder outlet were relaxed.

questions.stem: Sympathetic fibres in the hypogastric nerve (T12-L2) promote urine storage by

options.label: B
options.text: relaxing both detrusor and internal sphincter

options.label: C
options.text: relaxing the detrusor and contracting the bladder neck

options.label: D
options.text: contracting the detrusor and relaxing the bladder neck

questions.why: During bladder filling, sympathetic hypogastric pathways promote detrusor relaxation largely through beta-3 adrenergic receptors and increase bladder-neck smooth-muscle tone through alpha-1 receptors. These responses allow urine storage at relatively low bladder pressure.

notes.A: The micturition reflex activates sacral parasympathetic pathways and coordinated outlet relaxation, rather than being the primary sympathetic storage response.
notes.B: Relaxing bladder-neck smooth muscle would reduce outlet resistance; sympathetic storage activity generally maintains or increases its closure tone.
notes.D: Detrusor contraction with outlet relaxation describes coordinated voiding, which is principally associated with parasympathetic activation and withdrawal of storage pathways.
notes.E: The external urethral sphincter is primarily controlled by somatic pudendal motor neurons rather than direct hypogastric sympathetic innervation.

questions.stem: The supraspinal centre that coordinates the micturition reflex is located in the
questions.why: The pontine micturition centre coordinates the transition from storage to voiding by organising sacral parasympathetic activation and inhibition of sympathetic and somatic outlet pathways. Higher brain regions influence when this coordinated reflex is permitted.

notes.A: The sacral cord contains the spinal reflex circuits for bladder activity, but coordinated supraspinal control depends particularly on pontine pathways.
notes.B: The hypothalamus influences autonomic homeostasis but is not the principal centre coordinating detrusor contraction with urethral sphincter relaxation.
notes.C: The cerebellum contributes to motor coordination but does not serve as the conventional central switch coordinating bladder emptying.
notes.E: Medullary autonomic networks regulate several visceral functions, whereas the classic supraspinal voiding centre is located within the pons.

questions.stem: After normal voiding, the adult bladder typically retains a residual volume of about
questions.why: The bladder holds about 500 ml and leaves roughly 50 ml residual after voiding.

questions.stem: The glomerular filtration barrier, from blood to capsular space, consists of the

options.label: A
options.text: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane and podocyte slits

options.label: B
options.text: transitional epithelium, muscle layer and serosa

options.label: D
options.text: macula densa, mesangium and granular cells

options.label: E
options.text: brush border, basolateral membrane and tight junctions

questions.why: Glomerular filtrate crosses fenestrated capillary endothelium and its glycocalyx, the glomerular basement membrane, and slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes. Together these layers permit high water and small-solute permeability while restricting blood cells and most plasma proteins.

notes.B: Transitional epithelium lines urinary passages and is adapted to distension, rather than forming the specialised glomerular capillary filtration barrier.
notes.C: Endothelium, smooth muscle and adventitia describe layers of larger blood vessels; glomerular capillaries lack a continuous muscular coat.
notes.D: Macula densa, mesangial and granular cells participate in juxtaglomerular regulation, but do not form the three serial filtration layers.
notes.E: Brush borders and basolateral transport membranes characterise tubular epithelial reabsorption, downstream of the glomerular filtration barrier.

questions.stem: The negative charge carried by all three layers of the filtration barrier mainly acts to

options.label: A
options.text: reverse the direction of filtrate flow

options.label: B
options.text: retard the filtration of anionic molecules

options.label: C
options.text: attract and filter small cations preferentially

options.label: D
options.text: prevent water from crossing the membrane

options.label: E
options.text: increase the filtration of plasma proteins

questions.why: The fixed negative charge repels anions such as albumin, helping keep the filtrate protein-free.

questions.stem: Net filtration pressure in the glomerulus is calculated as glomerular hydrostatic pressure minus the sum of blood oncotic and capsular pressures, giving roughly
questions.why: With negligible oncotic pressure in normal Bowman space, net filtration pressure equals glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus capsular hydrostatic and glomerular plasma oncotic pressures. The stated example gives 55 minus 15 minus 30, or 10 mmHg.

notes.A: The assumed oncotic and capsular pressures of 10 mmHg each underestimate the conventional opposing forces used in this teaching example.
notes.B: Although the arithmetic gives 10 mmHg, the proposed values are not the stated conventional example and are not specifically restricted to standing.
notes.D: The opposing pressures of 15 and 30 mmHg total 45 mmHg, so subtracting them from 55 gives 10, not 20 mmHg.
notes.E: This calculation incorrectly uses a low value for glomerular driving pressure and produces negative filtration pressure rather than the conventional positive value.

questions.stem: The unusually high glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (about 55 mmHg) results from

options.label: A
options.text: the low resistance of the peritubular capillaries

options.label: B
options.text: the absence of a venous drainage from the glomerulus

options.label: C
options.text: direct connection of the glomerulus to the aorta

options.label: D
options.text: the efferent arteriole being narrower than the afferent

options.label: E
options.text: the afferent arteriole being narrower than the efferent

questions.why: A wider afferent and narrower efferent arteriole maintain a high pressure within the glomerular tuft.

questions.stem: A normal glomerular filtration rate of about 125 ml/min amounts to roughly how much filtrate per day?
questions.why: A filtration rate of 125 mL/min multiplied by 1,440 minutes per day yields 180,000 mL, or 180 litres daily. Extensive tubular reabsorption returns almost all of this filtrate to blood, leaving a much smaller urine volume.

notes.A: Eighteen litres would correspond to only one-tenth of the daily filtrate generated at the stated 125 mL/min rate.
notes.B: Approximately 1.8 litres is a plausible daily final urine volume after reabsorption, rather than the volume originally filtered by glomeruli.
notes.C: A daily filtrate of 1,800 litres is ten times the calculated volume and would require a filtration rate of 1,250 mL/min.
notes.D: Sixty litres per day corresponds to roughly 42 mL/min, substantially below the filtration rate specified in the question.

questions.stem: Renal autoregulation keeps GFR nearly constant over a mean arterial pressure range of about
questions.why: Renal myogenic responses and tubuloglomerular feedback maintain relatively stable renal blood flow and filtration across a conventional mean arterial pressure range of roughly 80–180 mmHg. The exact autoregulatory limits vary with physiological and disease conditions.

notes.B: Pressures of 40–80 mmHg extend below the usual lower autoregulatory limit, where renal perfusion and GFR can fall markedly.
notes.C: The range extending to 300 mmHg exceeds the conventional upper autoregulatory limit and may expose glomeruli to excessive pressure.
notes.D: Mean arterial pressures of 20–60 mmHg are generally too low to sustain normal renal filtration through autoregulation alone.
notes.E: Pressures of 180–260 mmHg extend above the usual autoregulatory range and cannot generally be compensated for by normal renal vascular responses.

questions.stem: The myogenic mechanism of renal autoregulation works because a rise in arterial pressure

options.label: A
options.text: stimulates renin release from granular cells

options.label: B
options.text: stretches the afferent arteriole, which then contracts

options.label: C
options.text: relaxes the afferent arteriole, increasing flow

options.label: D
options.text: dilates the efferent arteriole to drop pressure

options.label: E
options.text: closes the macula densa feedback loop

questions.why: Increased arterial pressure stretches afferent arteriolar smooth muscle, activating an intrinsic myogenic contraction through membrane depolarisation and calcium entry. The increased preglomerular resistance buffers transmission of elevated pressure to glomerular capillaries and stabilises filtration.

notes.A: Reduced rather than increased afferent arteriolar perfusion pressure generally stimulates renin release through the renal vascular pressure-sensing mechanism.
notes.C: Afferent dilatation would increase pressure transmission and blood flow, opposing the protective constriction elicited by increased vascular stretch.
notes.D: Efferent dilation can reduce glomerular pressure, but the primary renal myogenic response to increased pressure occurs in the afferent arteriole.
notes.E: Macula densa feedback is a separate tubular salt-sensing autoregulatory mechanism rather than the immediate intrinsic response of stretched smooth muscle.

questions.stem: In tubuloglomerular feedback, a rise in distal tubular NaCl detected by the macula densa leads to

options.label: A
options.text: renin release that raises systemic pressure

options.label: C
options.text: afferent arteriolar constriction that lowers GFR back to normal

options.label: D
options.text: afferent arteriolar dilatation that raises GFR further

options.label: E
options.text: efferent arteriolar constriction that raises GFR

questions.why: Increased sodium chloride delivery activates macula densa NKCC2 transport and promotes local ATP and adenosine signalling. Afferent arteriolar constriction reduces glomerular capillary pressure and filtration, providing negative feedback when distal tubular salt delivery rises.

notes.A: High macula densa sodium chloride delivery generally suppresses renin release rather than stimulating a systemic renin-mediated rise in pressure.
notes.B: Aldosterone acts through slower hormonal regulation of distal sodium transport, rather than providing the immediate afferent arteriolar response to increased salt delivery.
notes.D: Afferent dilatation would increase glomerular perfusion and tend to aggravate the increased tubular delivery, rather than providing negative feedback.
notes.E: Efferent constriction can increase glomerular pressure under some conditions, but high macula densa sodium chloride generally suppresses renin and promotes afferent constriction.

questions.stem: Renal clearance of a substance is defined as the

options.label: A
options.text: fraction of the substance reabsorbed in the tubule

options.label: B
options.text: rate at which urine is formed by the glomeruli

options.label: C
options.text: concentration of the substance in the final urine

options.label: D
options.text: volume of plasma completely cleared of it per unit time

options.label: E
options.text: mass of the substance filtered per minute

questions.why: Renal clearance is the hypothetical volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance by the kidneys per unit time. It equals urinary concentration multiplied by urine flow rate and divided by the substance's plasma concentration.

notes.A: The reabsorbed fraction describes the proportion of filtered substance reclaimed by tubules, rather than the hypothetical plasma volume cleared per minute.
notes.B: Glomerular filtration rate describes the volume of filtrate formed per unit time; clearance is substance-specific and depends on its renal handling.
notes.C: Urinary concentration is one component of the clearance equation, but alone cannot determine the plasma volume cleared per unit time.
notes.E: Filtered mass per minute equals GFR multiplied by filterable plasma concentration, whereas clearance is expressed as a volume per unit time.

questions.stem: Inulin is the ideal marker of GFR because it is

options.label: A
options.text: freely filtered and almost completely reabsorbed

options.label: B
options.text: secreted so heavily that none appears in blood

options.label: C
options.text: bound to plasma proteins and not filtered

options.label: D
options.text: produced endogenously at a constant rate

options.label: E
options.text: freely filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted

questions.why: Inulin is freely filtered through glomeruli and undergoes negligible tubular reabsorption, secretion or renal metabolism. Its urinary excretion therefore equals its filtered load, making its renal clearance a reference measure of glomerular filtration rate.

notes.A: A nearly completely reabsorbed marker has urinary excretion below its filtered load and would underestimate filtration rate rather than equal it.
notes.B: Extensive tubular secretion adds substance beyond its filtered load and would cause clearance to exceed GFR, rather than isolate glomerular filtration.
notes.C: Strong plasma protein binding prevents free glomerular filtration, so clearance of such a marker cannot directly represent the total filtered plasma volume.
notes.D: Endogenous production is a useful practical property of creatinine, whereas inulin is an administered marker whose accuracy depends on its renal handling.

questions.stem: If the clearance of a substance is greater than that of inulin, the substance must be
questions.why: For an ordinarily filterable substance under steady-state conditions, clearance greater than inulin clearance means urinary excretion exceeds the amount that filtration alone could provide. Net tubular secretion therefore contributes additional substance to the tubular fluid.

notes.B: Complete tubular reabsorption would leave negligible substance in final urine and produce a clearance near zero, not greater than GFR.
notes.C: A freely filtered substance with neither secretion nor reabsorption has clearance approximately equal to inulin, rather than exceeding it.
notes.D: Albumin binding restricts the freely filterable fraction of a substance and does not by itself explain urinary clearance exceeding glomerular filtration rate.
notes.E: Intracellular metabolism can alter the amount of substance available for excretion, but does not establish the net tubular addition required by the conventional clearance interpretation.

questions.stem: Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is used to estimate renal plasma flow because it is

options.label: A
options.text: bound to red cells rather than plasma

options.label: B
options.text: almost completely cleared in a single pass

options.label: C
options.text: entirely reabsorbed so none is excreted

options.label: D
options.text: filtered but not secreted at all

questions.why: At low plasma concentrations, para-aminohippurate is filtered and efficiently secreted by proximal tubules, removing most of the PAH delivered to functioning renal tissue in one pass. Its clearance therefore estimates effective renal plasma flow, rather than exact total flow.

notes.A: PAH clearance is calculated from its plasma concentration and urinary excretion; preferential red-cell binding is not the basis of its high extraction.
notes.C: Complete reabsorption would prevent urinary elimination and yield negligible clearance, rather than allowing estimation of renal plasma delivery.
notes.D: Filtration alone would make clearance approximate GFR, whereas substantial proximal tubular secretion allows PAH clearance to approach effective renal plasma flow.
notes.E: Creatinine arises endogenously from muscle creatine metabolism; PAH is an administered organic anion used for estimating renal plasma flow.

questions.stem: Creatinine is commonly used instead of inulin to estimate GFR clinically because it is

options.label: A
options.text: entirely secreted by the distal tubule

options.label: B
options.text: bound to plasma proteins and unfiltered

options.label: C
options.text: endogenous, filtered and only slightly secreted

options.label: D
options.text: not present in the body unless infused

options.label: E
options.text: heavily reabsorbed in the proximal tubule

questions.why: Creatinine is produced endogenously from creatine metabolism and is freely filtered, with a variable small additional contribution from tubular secretion. Creatinine clearance therefore provides a practical estimate of GFR, although it tends to overestimate true filtration.

notes.A: Creatinine enters tubular fluid substantially through glomerular filtration, with some secretion, rather than being entirely secreted by distal tubular cells.
notes.B: Creatinine is largely freely filterable and does not depend on strong plasma protein binding for its clinical use as a filtration marker.
notes.D: Creatinine is continuously generated in the body, which avoids the need for an infusion required by some exogenous filtration markers.
notes.E: Substantial proximal reabsorption would cause clearance to underestimate GFR, whereas creatinine usually undergoes modest net tubular secretion.

questions.stem: Renal blood flow is obtained from renal plasma flow using the haematocrit by the relation
questions.why: Renal plasma flow represents the plasma fraction of total renal blood flow. Since the fractional haematocrit represents the cellular volume fraction, dividing renal plasma flow by one minus haematocrit converts plasma flow into total blood flow.

notes.A: Haematocrit represents the erythrocyte volume fraction, not the plasma fraction needed to convert renal plasma flow into whole-blood flow.
notes.B: Multiplying plasma flow by the red-cell fraction would produce a smaller quantity, rather than recovering total blood flow from its plasma component.
notes.C: Renal plasma flow has units of volume per time, whereas haematocrit is dimensionless; adding them does not yield a meaningful flow.
notes.E: Multiplying by the plasma fraction converts whole-blood flow to plasma flow, but the reverse calculation requires division by that fraction.

questions.stem: Across the whole nephron, roughly what proportion of the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed back into the blood?
questions.why: Approximately 180 litres of filtrate are formed daily at a typical adult GFR, but only about one to two litres are excreted as urine. Thus roughly 99% of filtered water is reclaimed along the nephron.

notes.A: Reabsorbing only half of the filtrate would leave approximately 90 litres of urine per day, far above the normal daily output.
notes.B: Approximately 65% of filtered sodium and water is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule alone; subsequent nephron segments reclaim much more.
notes.C: Reabsorbing one-quarter of the filtrate would leave most filtered water in urine and is incompatible with normal renal water conservation.
notes.D: Ten per cent reabsorption would leave approximately 162 litres daily at a 180-litre filtration rate, rather than the normal small urine volume.

questions.stem: Sodium reabsorption consumes about 80% of the kidney's energy because it depends on the

options.label: D
options.text: aquaporin channels of the collecting duct

options.label: E
options.text: Cl-/HCO3- exchanger in the proximal tubule

questions.why: Basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase actively pumps Na+ out of the cell, creating the gradient that drives most tubular transport.

questions.stem: Unlike glucose, the reabsorption of sodium does not show a transport maximum because it

options.label: A
options.text: relies on a single low-capacity carrier

options.label: B
options.text: it is pumped all along the tubule

options.label: C
options.text: is reabsorbed only in the proximal tubule

questions.why: Na+ is handled all along the tubule by abundant pumps, so it has no single saturable Tm like glucose.

questions.stem: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs approximately what fraction of filtered sodium and water?
questions.why: The PCT reabsorbs roughly 65% of filtered Na+ and water (and essentially all glucose and amino acids).

questions.stem: Glucose, amino acids and most organic nutrients are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by

options.label: A
options.text: primary active transport using their own ATPases

options.label: D
options.text: secondary active cotransport coupled to sodium

options.label: E
options.text: simple diffusion down their own gradients

questions.why: These solutes are cotransported with Na+ as it moves down its gradient — secondary active transport.

questions.stem: A transport maximum sets a renal threshold because

options.label: A
options.text: the substance can no longer be filtered at the glomerulus

options.label: B
options.text: the tubule stops reabsorbing water as well

options.label: C
options.text: secretion into the lumen ceases entirely

options.label: D
options.text: the substance is destroyed within the tubule cell

options.label: E
options.text: once the carriers are saturated, the excess substance is excreted

questions.why: When carrier proteins are saturated at the Tm, any filtered load above that spills into the urine.

questions.stem: The descending limb of the loop of Henle is characterised by being

options.label: A
options.text: permeable to water but not to solute

options.label: B
options.text: permeable to solute but not to water

options.label: C
options.text: permeable to both water and solute equally

options.label: D
options.text: impermeable to both water and solute

options.label: E
options.text: the main site of active Na+ pumping

questions.why: Water leaves the water-permeable descending limb osmotically, while solute stays, concentrating the filtrate toward the bend.

questions.stem: The main luminal carrier bringing sodium into the cells of the thick ascending limb is the
questions.why: The thick ascending limb uses the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (the target of loop diuretics).

questions.stem: At the bend of the loop of Henle in a juxtamedullary nephron, the tubular fluid reaches an osmolality of about
questions.why: Water loss along the descending limb concentrates the fluid to about 1200 mOsm at the hairpin tip.

questions.stem: By the time tubular fluid reaches the early distal convoluted tubule it is hypotonic (about 100 mOsm) because the ascending limb has

options.label: A
options.text: secreted extra solute into the lumen

options.label: B
options.text: added aquaporins to let water in

options.label: D
options.text: pumped out NaCl while impermeable to water

questions.why: The water-impermeable ascending limb removes NaCl, diluting the fluid to about 100 mOsm.

questions.stem: The vasa recta act as a countercurrent exchanger that chiefly serves to

options.label: A
options.text: generate the medullary gradient by pumping NaCl

options.label: B
options.text: filter plasma a second time in the medulla

options.label: C
options.text: secrete renin in response to low flow

options.label: D
options.text: reabsorb all the glucose escaping the PCT

questions.why: The hairpin vasa recta supply the medulla yet, by countercurrent exchange, avoid washing out its hypertonicity.

questions.stem: Antidiuretic hormone concentrates the urine by

options.label: A
options.text: inserting aquaporins into the collecting duct

options.label: B
options.text: pumping sodium out of the ascending limb

questions.why: ADH (vasopressin) acts via cAMP to insert aquaporins into collecting-duct principal cells, raising water reabsorption.

questions.stem: The stimulus that most directly triggers ADH release is

options.label: A
options.text: a rise in arterial oxygen tension

options.label: D
options.text: a rise in distal tubular NaCl

questions.why: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect rising osmolality and drive posterior-pituitary release of ADH (angiotensin II also stimulates it).

questions.stem: The high blood glucose of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus produces an osmotic diuresis because glucose

options.label: C
options.text: exceeds its Tm and holds water in the tubule

questions.why: Once filtered glucose exceeds the reabsorptive Tm, the unreabsorbed glucose osmotically retains water in the tubule.

questions.stem: Furosemide (lasix) produces diuresis by inhibiting the

options.label: B
options.text: carbonic anhydrase of the proximal tubule

options.label: C
options.text: epithelial Na+ channel of the distal tubule

options.label: D
options.text: Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter of the thick ascending limb

options.label: E
options.text: Na+-glucose cotransporter of the proximal tubule

questions.why: Loop diuretics block the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the medullary thick ascending limb.

questions.stem: Alcohol promotes diuresis mainly by

options.label: A
options.text: blocking sodium reabsorption in the loop

options.label: C
options.text: acting as a non-reabsorbed osmotic agent

options.label: E
options.text: inhibiting the secretion of antidiuretic hormone

questions.why: Alcohol suppresses ADH release, reducing collecting-duct water reabsorption.

questions.stem: Potassium is handled along the nephron such that it is

options.label: A
options.text: reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and secreted in the distal tubule

options.label: B
options.text: secreted in the proximal tubule and reabsorbed distally

options.label: E
options.text: reabsorbed equally along the whole tubule

questions.why: K+ is reabsorbed unregulated in the PCT and secreted, under aldosterone control, in the distal tubule and collecting duct.

questions.stem: Renin released from the kidney acts on its substrate to produce
questions.why: Renin converts liver-derived angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

questions.stem: Angiotensin-converting enzyme, which forms angiotensin II from angiotensin I, is found chiefly in the
questions.why: ACE in the lungs converts angiotensin I to the active angiotensin II.

questions.stem: Which action is NOT produced by angiotensin II?
questions.why: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor, not a vasodilator; it also drives thirst, aldosterone, ADH and mesangial contraction.

questions.stem: Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron to

options.label: E
options.text: reabsorb sodium and water, secrete potassium

questions.why: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex increases Na+ (and water) reabsorption and K+ secretion in the distal tubule and collecting duct.

questions.stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide opposes the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system by
questions.why: ANP promotes natriuresis and diuresis, lowering blood volume and opposing RAAS.

questions.stem: Renin secretion by the granular cells is stimulated by

options.label: B
options.text: a fall in renal perfusion pressure

options.label: E
options.text: a high distal tubular NaCl load

questions.why: Low perfusion pressure, sympathetic drive and low macula densa NaCl all stimulate renin release.

questions.stem: The kidneys keep the osmotic concentration of body fluids close to
questions.why: Plasma osmolality is held near 300 mOsm by regulated water and solute handling.

questions.stem: A convenient physiological way to view acid-base handling is that reabsorbing a bicarbonate ion is equivalent to
questions.why: Because HCO3- buffers H+, reclaiming HCO3- is equivalent to removing H+ (and losing HCO3- equals gaining H+).

questions.stem: The most important buffer system of the blood plasma (extracellular fluid) is the
questions.why: The bicarbonate/carbonic acid pair is the principal ECF buffer; phosphate dominates urine and ICF, protein the cells.

questions.stem: The phosphate buffer system is most important as a buffer of the
questions.why: Phosphate is concentrated in urine and cells, where it buffers effectively; it is minor in plasma.

questions.stem: Proteins such as haemoglobin can buffer both acids and bases because they are

options.label: A
options.text: unable to change charge with pH

options.label: B
options.text: amphoteric - they donate and accept H+

options.label: D
options.text: strong bases that bind all H+

questions.why: Amino acid side groups let proteins release or take up H+ depending on pH, making them amphoteric buffers.

questions.stem: Movement of bicarbonate out of the red cell in exchange for chloride, during CO2 transport, is known as the
questions.why: The HCO3-/Cl- antiport across the red-cell membrane is the chloride shift, or Hamburger effect.

questions.stem: Only the kidney can rid the body of which type of acid?

options.label: C
options.text: all acids are handled by the lungs

questions.why: The lungs excrete the volatile acid (CO2); only the kidneys eliminate fixed, non-volatile acids.

questions.stem: Reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate in the proximal tubule depends on secretion of H+, which in the lumen

options.label: B
options.text: is excreted unchanged as free acid

options.label: D
options.text: is reabsorbed together with the bicarbonate

options.label: E
options.text: joins HCO3- to form CO2 and water

questions.why: Secreted H+ joins filtered HCO3- to make H2CO3, which becomes CO2 + H2O; these enter the cell and regenerate HCO3- for reabsorption.

questions.stem: Generation of new bicarbonate linked to ammonium excretion uses the amino acid
questions.why: Tubular metabolism of glutamine produces two NH4+ (excreted) and two new HCO3- (added to blood) per molecule.

questions.stem: In a patient with respiratory acidosis the typical arterial picture is

options.label: A
options.text: pH normal with a low PaCO2 and low bicarbonate

options.label: B
options.text: pH below 7.35 with a raised PaCO2 and initially normal bicarbonate

options.label: C
options.text: pH above 7.45 with a low PaCO2

options.label: D
options.text: pH below 7.35 with a low bicarbonate and normal PaCO2

options.label: E
options.text: pH above 7.45 with a raised bicarbonate

questions.why: Hypoventilation retains CO2: pH < 7.35, PaCO2 > 45 mmHg, with bicarbonate normal until renal compensation.

questions.stem: Metabolic acidosis (for example from diabetic ketoacidosis) is characterised by

options.label: A
options.text: a normal bicarbonate with a low PaCO2

options.label: B
options.text: a raised bicarbonate with a raised PaCO2

options.label: C
options.text: a low bicarbonate with a normal PaCO2

options.label: D
options.text: a raised PaCO2 with a normal bicarbonate

options.label: E
options.text: a raised bicarbonate with a low PaCO2

questions.why: Metabolic acidosis lowers HCO3- below 22 mEq/L while PaCO2 stays normal until respiratory compensation begins.

questions.stem: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis occurs within minutes and consists of

options.label: D
options.text: increased ventilation that drives off CO2

questions.why: The lungs hyperventilate to blow off CO2, restoring the HCO3-/H2CO3 ratio toward 20:1 within minutes.

questions.stem: The absolute blood pH limits compatible with life are approximately
questions.why: Survival is possible only within a pH of roughly 7.0 to 7.8; beyond these, coma or tetany and death follow.

questions.stem: In the collecting duct, the cells that secrete bicarbonate during alkalosis are the
questions.why: Type B intercalated cells secrete HCO3- (and reabsorb H+) in alkalosis, the reverse of type A cells.
